docs.title: Day 1: Linux Fundamentals for Biologists
docs.text: Welcome to your first day of the IBDC-HPC Workshop. Today, we bridge the gap between biological data and computational power.

docs.title: 1. Why Linux for Biology? (30 mins)
docs.text:
Traditional operating systems often fail when handling large-scale genomic data.

  • Massive File Handling: Linux can read a 50GB FASTQ file in milliseconds, whereas Excel or Notepad would crash.
  • Stability: Linux systems are built to run for months, perfect for long-running bioinformatics pipelines.
  • Reproducibility: Every command you type can be saved in a script, ensuring your experiment can be repeated exactly by others.

docs.title: 2. Navigating the "Digital Lab" (The Map)
docs.text: Think of the Linux directory tree as your lab's storage room. Everything starts from the Root (/).

docs.title: Essential Navigation Commands
docs.text: Command Biology Context What it does pwd "Which shelf am I at?" Print Working Directory (shows your current path). ls -lh "Check the inventory." List files with human-readable sizes (MB/GB). cd "Walk to a new room." Change Directory (e.g., cd raw_data/). mkdir "Set up a new bench." Make Directory (e.g., mkdir mouse_project).

docs.title: 3. Managing Data Without a Mouse (The Action)
docs.text: In bioinformatics, we rarely click "Save As." Instead, we use commands to manipulate files.

docs.title: Viewing Data
docs.text:
• Peek at DNA reads: Don't open the whole file; just look at the top.
    • head -n 4 sample.fastq (Shows the first sequence read).
  • Check the end of a log:
    • tail -n 10 analysis.log (See if your process finished).

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
• Back up raw data: Always keep a copy before you start filtering.
    • cp raw_seq.fastq raw_seq_backup.fastq.
  • Organizing files:
    • mv results.txt ./final_output/ (Moves the file to the results folder).
  • Deleting (Warning!):
    • rm temp_file.txt (There is no recycle bin in Linux. It is gone forever!).

docs.title: 4. Practical Hands-on Exercise (60 mins)
docs.text:
Follow these steps in your terminal to create your first workspace.

  1. Create your folder: mkdir workshop_practice
  2. Enter the folder: cd workshop_practice
  3. Create a dummy sequence: echo "ATGCATGCATGC" > dna_sequence.txt
  4. Confirm the file exists: ls -l
  5. Check your current location: pwd (Ensure you see /home/harsha/workshop_practice).

docs.title: 5. Pro-Tips for Speed
docs.text:
• Tab Completion: Type the first 3 letters of a folder name and hit Tab. Linux will finish the word for you!.
  • Command History: Use the Up Arrow key to find commands you typed earlier.
  • Naming Rule: Never use spaces in filenames (e.g., use mouse_data.txt, not mouse data.txt).

docs.title: Day 1: Linux Command Reference for Biologists
docs.text:
In Linux, data is organized into files and directories (folders). While you can use a Graphical User Interface (GUI), most bioinformatics tools require the Terminal (Ctrl + Alt + T).

Note: Use man <command> to view the manual for any tool. Press q to exit the manual.

Notation: $ indicates the prompt (do not type it). # indicates a comment.

docs.title: Listing Files (ls)
docs.text:
• # List files in a directory $ ls
  • # List files one per line $ ls -1
  • # Long format (with details and human-readable sizes) $ ls -lh
  • # Sort by time modified (newest first) $ ls -lt

docs.title: Handling Directories (cd, mkdir, pwd)
docs.text:
• # Change to a specific directory $ cd my_folder
  • # Go to the home directory $ cd
  • # Go up to the parent directory $ cd ..
  • # Get the present working directory path $ pwd
  • # Create a new directory $ mkdir new_folder

docs.title: Copy, Move, and Delete (cp, mv, rm)
docs.text:
• # Copy a file $ cp file1 file_copy
  • # Rename a file $ mv old_name new_name
  • # Delete a file (Warning: No Recycle Bin!) $ rm file1

docs.title: Quick Peeks (head, tail, cat)
docs.text:
• # Print first 10 lines $ head sample.fastq
  • # Print last 50 lines $ tail -n 50 sample.fastq
  • # Remove headers (print starting from line 2) $ tail -n +2 data.tsv
  • # Merge two files into one $ cat file1 file2 > file3

docs.title: Word and Line Counting (wc)
docs.text: • # Count lines in a file (useful for counting sequences) $ wc -l reads.fastq

docs.title: Extracting Columns (cut)
docs.text: • # Get 1st and 4th columns from a tab-separated file $ cut -f 1,4 file.tsv

docs.title: Sorting Data (sort)
docs.text:
• # Numerical sort on the 4th column $ sort -nr -k 4 file1
  • # Version sort (ideal for chromosomes: chr1, chr2, chr10) $ sort -V file1

docs.title: Advanced Manipulation (awk, grep)
docs.text:
• # Calculate difference between columns 3 and 2 $ awk '{print $3-$2}' file.bed
  • # Search for a specific gene or chromosome $ grep -w 'chr1' peaks.tsv

docs.title: 4. Meta Characters & Pipes
docs.text:
• Wildcards (*): Match any characters. $ ls *.fastq (Lists all fastq files).
  • Redirection (>): Save output to a file. $ ls *.txt > file_list.
  • The Pipe (|): Use the output of one command as the input for the next. $ ls *.fastq | wc -l (Count how many fastq files exist).

docs.title: 5. Compressed Files (Bioinformatics Standard)
docs.text:
• # Compress a file $ gzip reads.fastq
  • # View a compressed file without unzipping $ zcat reads.fastq.gz | head

docs.title: Linux Foundations for Biologists: Lab Bench to CLI
docs.text: [cite_start]This guide covers the core mechanics of the Linux operating system used in high-throughput biology[cite: 2].

docs.title: 1. Under the Hood: Linux Architecture
docs.text:
The Shell is your bridge. [cite_start]It negotiates with the Kernel to execute commands on the Hardware[cite: 55].

  • [cite_start]Hardware: CPU, RAM, and Storage (HDD/SSD)[cite: 54].
  • [cite_start]Kernel: The "Brain" and Resource Manager[cite: 52].
  • [cite_start]The Shell: The Interpreter and Translator[cite: 49].
  • [cite_start]User & Utilities: This is where you work![cite: 47].

docs.title: 2. Decoding the Interface
docs.text:
[cite_start]When you look at the terminal, the Prompt tells you exactly where you are and who you are[cite: 57].

  • [cite_start]ibdc: Current User[cite: 63].
  • [cite_start]cluster: Hostname (Server Name)[cite: 65].
  • [cite_start]~: Current Location (Home Directory)[cite: 68].
  • [cite_start]$: The prompt, ready for your input[cite: 69].

docs.title: 3. The Anatomy of a Command
docs.text:
Commands follow a strict grammar. [cite_start]A mistake in a space or a dash will cause the command to fail[cite: 71, 79].

ls -l --sort time Documents/

  • [cite_start]Command: The "Verb" (What to do)[cite: 74].
  • [cite_start]Short/Long Options: The "Switches" (Settings like sorting or long-listing)[cite: 74, 75].
  • [cite_start]Argument: The "Object" (What to act upon, e.g., a folder or file)[cite: 77].

docs.title: 4. The "Holy Trinity" of Navigation
docs.text:
[cite_start]Master these three to never get lost in your data[cite: 115].

  1. pwd: "Where am I?" (Print Working Directory) [cite_start][cite: 116].
  2. ls: "What is here?" (List files) [cite_start][cite: 118].
  3. [cite_start]cd: "Take me there" (Change Directory)[cite: 119].

docs.title: 5. Biology File Operations
docs.text:
[cite_start]Managing large-scale genomic datasets safely[cite: 135].

Action Command Biology Example Creation mkdir / touch [cite_start]mkdir sequencing_reads[cite: 138]. Organization cp / mv [cite_start]cp sample_R1.fq backup/[cite: 139]. Inspection head / tail [cite_start]head -n 20 reads.fastq[cite: 185]. Search grep [cite_start]grep 'GeneID:12345' records.txt[cite: 194].

⚠️ Danger Zone: Deleting is permanent. [cite_start]There is no 'Recycle Bin' in the CLI[cite: 148].
